finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id authorization check is not awaited, so any authenticated user can delete any report.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled :id path param on DELETE /reports/:id (server.js:18), authenticated only via req.session.user (server.js:5).

trace.note: DELETE route handler entry, :id from attacker
authorize(req.user,'delete',report) called without await; returned promise discarded
authorize is async; throws 403 at lines 11-14 as a rejected promise
remove executes regardless of grant result

finding.guards_checked: authorize grant check (server.js:9-16) is enforced in its own body but its result never gates the delete. PUT handler at server.js:27 correctly awaits authorize, so this is a per-route inconsistency. Unhandled rejection from a denied check can also crash Node >=15 (not runtime-verified).

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 is the only access control. It throws a 403 on a failed grant, but the DELETE handler calls it at server.js:20 without await or a try/catch, so the rejection never gates line 21's db.reports.remove(report.id). The PUT handler at server.js:27 does await it, so the check works there.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at server.js:20 discards authorize()'s promise, so db.reports.remove at server.js:21 runs before the grant check at server.js:10-15 can reject, and the 204 at server.js:22 follows regardless. Only server.js is in the directory, so session setup, the db module, and any route-level auth middleware are not visible; the claim that the attacker is "authenticated" is not enforced in this file, but the bypass holds for whichever caller reaches the route.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire req.body to db.reports.update with no field allowlist (mass assignment).
finding.source: JSON body parsed by express.json() (server.js:3) on PUT /reports/:id (server.js:25).

trace.note: await authorize(req.user,'write',report) passes for users with write grant
update receives full req.body, no field restriction

finding.guards_checked: Authorization on the report (server.js:27) is enforced. No field-level allowlist or schema validation exists in this file. Impact depends on the db schema (e.g. owner/tenant/grants fields), which is not in the repo, so impact is uncertain.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` checks a write grant on this report and throws (403) on failure, so only users with a write grant on the specific report reach server.js:28. No field allowlist or schema validation exists anywhere in server.js, and no db schema is in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (express.json at server.js:3, get at :26, awaited authorize at :27, unfiltered db.reports.update(report.id, req.body) at :28), and a write-grant holder can reach the sink, but whether mass assignment is exploitable depends on which columns db.reports.update accepts (owner, tenant, grants) and the schema is not in the repo, so I cannot decide the impact from this code.

finding.claim: Nonexistent report id yields null report, causing a TypeError in authorize (resource.id) and an unhandled promise rejection in the async route handlers.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled :id path param on DELETE or PUT /reports/:id (server.js:18, 25).
finding.sink: resource.id at server.js:10 and report.id at server.js:21, 28

trace.note: db.reports.get returns null for unknown id (DELETE)
resource.id throws TypeError, rejecting authorize promise
same pattern on PUT; rejection propagates through await at line 27

finding.guards_checked: No null check after db.reports.get at server.js:19 or :26. Severity depends on Express version (Express 4 does not catch async rejections; Express 5 does). Version not in repo, so lower confidence.

verdict.guard_found: none. No null check after db.reports.get at server.js:19 or :26. The only other control is the session-derived req.user at server.js:5, which is not a guard for a null report. The DELETE path also has no await on authorize at server.js:20, so the 403 never blocks the removal at :21.
verdict.reason: The downstream path is accurate: authorize dereferences resource.id at server.js:10 and the handlers dereference report.id at server.js:21 and :28, but `db` is never defined or required in server.js, so whether db.reports.get returns null for an unknown id (server.js:19, :26) cannot be checked from the repo, and the impact depends on the unknown Express version. The claim's attacker is any user with a session (server.js:5), and separately, the missing await at server.js:20 means a user lacking the delete grant can still delete an existing report, which is a more serious issue than the one claimed.
